newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. African assembly adopts abortion law.
newsitem.headline: S. African assembly adopts abortion law.

text.p: The National Assembly of South Africa's parliament on Wednesday approved a bill that will give the country one of the most liberal laws on abortion in the world.

The bill, which will allow state-funded abortion on demand, was approved by 209 votes to 87 with five abstentions. The bill next week goes before the African National Congress-dominated Senate but passage is assured as the ANC has told its members they must vote for it.
Among those who supported The Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Bill was Sister Bernard Ncube, a Catholic nun and a legislator for the ANC.
ANC members cheered and ululated in joy at the adoption of the most controversial law so far put to the country's fledgling democratic parliament.
Members of the white-led National Party sat stony-faced and rightist Freedom Front leader Constand Viljoen shook his head.

National Party spokeswoman Sheila Camerer said after the vote that her party would seek legal advice on whether the bill violated South Africa's new constitution and its right-to-life guarantee used to outlaw capital punishment.
Despite the ANC's orders to its MPs, Catholic priest Smangaliso Mkhatshwa -- an ANC activist and legislator who was repeatedly detained and tortured under apartheid -- stayed away.
Mkhatshwa told reporters a few days before the vote he was still wrestling with his conscience on whether to obey his party and support the bill or obey his church and oppose it.
The Catholic Church was one of the fiercest critics of the bill during two sessions of emotional public hearings.
The bill clears the way for state-funded abortion on demand during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy and subject to some conditions for a further eight weeks.

The draft law gives women and even minor children the sole right to decide whether to have an abortion and specifically states that they need not consult partners or parents. Currently abortion is only allowed after rape or for women whose health is seriously at risk.
Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma told reporters it could be several months before the bill was promulgated into law.
